title: SDK graceful degradation and tool telemetry playbook (PRD draft)
content:
Purpose
This PRD sketch proposes a coordinated set of runtime and SDK ergonomics changes to improve how Hosted API clients handle: 1) partial/streaming outputs, 2) tool calling handshakes, and 3) graceful fallback under capacity or model-variant degradation — all while emitting lightweight telemetry that surfaces cost/latency tradeoffs to product teams.

Problem statement
Customers integrating streaming hosted responses frequently struggle with three pain points:
- brittle client behavior when partial tokens or structured fragments arrive out-of-order or are truncated, leading to UI jank and incorrect tool invocations;
- no consistent pattern for confirming tool-call contracts in streaming flows (racey tool handshakes across websockets/HTTP);
- poor visibility into when degradations happen (e.g., model downgraded, cache miss, slow KV loads) and limited client-side options to mitigate (fallback prompts, reduced sampling).

Goals
- Define a small, practical handshake + streaming delivery pattern that SDKs can implement with minimal surface area and sockets overhead.
- Provide an explicit, composable graceful-degradation mode for SDKs and server routing that preserves client UX (partial results, confidence hints, fallback tokens).
- Surface per-request telemetry fields (latency breakdown, fallback reason, model-variant, token-count delta) so customers can instrument and tune.
- Keep protocol backwards-compatible; allow gradual rollout with feature flags.

Non-goals
- Replacing existing chunked streaming APIs (we extend them with metadata, not rewrite).
- Heavyweight runtime changes (avoid large server-side refactors in first phase).

User scenarios
1) Messaging app: progressive paragraphs stream in; user can click an inline "run calculator" tool that must only be invoked after the model signals a structured tool intent. Client must avoid duplicate invocations if the sequence reconnects.
2) Analytics assistant: long-generation summary is streaming; backend decides to fallback from a large model to a small quantized variant because of load — client should receive a single coherent status that allows it to show a degraded quality badge and keep streaming tokens.
3) Form-generator: model yields a JSON-like schema in fragments; SDK must buffer partial object keys until a complete object is emitted or a commit signal occurs.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics
- SDKs implement handshake and degradation flags in at least two official languages (JS, Python) within 8 weeks of spec approval.
- Number of duplicate tool invocations recorded by telemetry drops by >= 80% on pilot customers.
- Customers can differentiate degradation causes in 90% of failed or downgraded requests via telemetry.
- No increase in median end-to-end latency > 5% for streaming calls in canary.

Design proposal (high level)
1) Stream metadata envelope
Every streaming message can optionally include an immutable metadata header that is separate from token payloads. Header fields (min set):
- seq: monotonic integer for ordering
- fragment_type: [TOKEN, STRUCTURE_OPEN, STRUCTURE_CLOSE, TOOL_INTENT, TOOL_CONFIRM, FINAL_STATUS, DEGRADATION_NOTICE]
- model_variant: short id (e.g., gptx-10b-q8)
- fallback_reason: one of [none, capacity, timeout, sampling_error, model_unavailable, operator_action]
- confidence_hint: float (0-1) as a soft signal clients can surface
Note: if header absent, client retains legacy behavior (just tokens).

2) Tool-call handshake (stream-first flow)
- TOOL_INTENT fragment: model emits a single TOOL_INTENT fragment containing a compact tool descriptor (tool_id, minimal arg schema or sample args, optional invocation_hint). The SDK should pause automatic invocation and surface an "intent confirmation" event to the app.
- Client may confirm invocation by sending a control message confirm_tool_call {intent_seq, caller_id, arg_overrides}. The server routes confirm to the tool-execution layer.
- TOOL_CONFIRM fragment: server streams back TOOL_CONFIRM with execution_status and tool_output_ref. This is treated as part of the stream and can resume token streaming.
Edge behavior: if connection drops before confirm, the SDK should allow re-delivery of stored TOOL_INTENT only once (idempotency token included). If duplicate confirm is sent, tool infra must be idempotent (we add an invocation_id).

3) Structured partials and commit signals
- STRUCTURE_OPEN and STRUCTURE_CLOSE fragments allow the SDK to maintain a light-weight parser that reconstructs objects without waiting for full finalization.
- FINAL_STATUS fragment signals that the server considers the generation for this response complete (even if reconnects arrive later). Clients should use FINAL_STATUS to commit or render final UI state.

4) Graceful degradation mode (server + SDK interplay)
- Server can inject DEGRADATION_NOTICE with fallback_reason and model_variant that indicates a switch or partial fallback.
- SDK behavior modes (configurable per-call):
  - "transparent": continue streaming tokens and annotate UI with a non-blocking badge when DEGRADATION_NOTICE occurs;
  - "strict": pause further streaming and surface a confirmation UI asking user to accept lower-quality continuation;
  - "rollback": abort current response and request a restart on a pinned model variant.
Default should be "transparent" to minimize user friction.

5) Telemetry fields (lightweight)
At the end of the call (or on FINAL_STATUS), server emits a telemetry summary block with these fields:
- total_tokens (num)
- model_variant (id)
- fallback_reason (enum)
- latency_ms (total), kv_cache_miss_ms, tool_exec_ms (best-effort)
- duplicated_tool_invokes (count)
These should be exposed via SDK callbacks and included in hosted logs for tenant dashboards.

API surface and SDK ergonomics (JS + Python patterns)
- Streaming client exposes two parallel event streams: tokens/onToken(cb) and control/onControl(cb). Control events include TOOL_INTENT, TOOL_CONFIRM, DEGRADATION_NOTICE, FINAL_STATUS.
- High-level helper: onToolIntent(intent, {autoConfirm:false, idempotencyKey:null}) -> returns a promise that resolves when tool confirmation occurs or rejects on timeout.
- Structured helper: stream.parseJsonFragments(onObject) which emits partial objects when STRUCTURE_CLOSE completes an object.
- Config flags: {degradationMode: 'transparent'|'strict'|'rollback', telemetry: boolean, maxReplays: 1} passed per-call.

Backward compatibility and rollout plan
Phase 1 (server-side flag + opt-in SDK): server emits control headers only when client sends header_accepts_control=true. This avoids breaking older clients.
Phase 2 (broad roll): enable control headers by default and add lightweight client libraries shipping handlers.
Phase 3 (enrich telemetry): include more fine-grained latency fields and a sampled trace id.

Operational concerns
- Idempotency: ensure tool invocation includes invocation_id and the tool platform enforces at-least-once semantics with de-duplication TTL.
- Cost telemetry: sampling telemetry at 1% for verbose fields to avoid per-request overhead.
- Security: tool descriptors must not leak secrets; confirm messages must be authenticated to the user.

Open questions / risks
- How do we represent nested structures that span multiple open/close fragments? (parser complexity vs. client memory)
- Do we need a formal schema language for tool descriptors, or is a minimal sample+type enough?
- SDKs for mobile platforms may need binary-compact envelopes — should we define a binary wire format later?

Implementation checklist (MVP)
- [ ] server: add metadata envelope support and optional control header (canary region).
- [ ] server: emit TOOL_INTENT + FINAL_STATUS for test model.
- [ ] sdk-js: implement onControl events + onToolIntent helper.
- [ ] sdk-py: streaming iterator yields control messages as separate items.
- [ ] telemetry: add summary block at FINAL_STATUS and sample detailed traces.
- [ ] docs: publish "Playbook: graceful-degradation and tool telemetry" and migration guide.

Migration notes for customers
- Existing applications will keep working. To opt-in, set header_accepts_control=true and use new SDK handlers. Start in transparent mode to assess frequency of fallbacks. Use telemetry to determine if strict or rollback modes are needed.

Appendix: example control sequence (simplified)
1) client connects and requests stream with header_accepts_control=true.
2) server streams tokens (seq 1..n) then emits TOOL_INTENT (seq n+1).
3) UI shows tool intent, user taps confirm, SDK sends confirm_tool_call referencing intent seq n+1.
4) tool executes; server emits TOOL_CONFIRM with tool_output_ref.
5) server resumes token streaming and ends with FINAL_STATUS.
6) telemetry summary block is emitted with fallback_reason=none.

Notes to reviewers
- Focus feedback on the control envelope fields and the default SDK degradationMode. We deliberately picked a minimal header to reduce client parsing complexity.
- If you have concerns about the idempotency approach or mobile wire size, flag them in PR comments.
